title: Four Tasks Over One Spanish Passage
takeaway: The passage's language, Spanish, appears in the J-lens readouts at similar rates during all four tasks, but swapping it to French changes the model's answer only under explicit report and flexible computation. Continuation and anomaly detection produce the same output either way, so the workspace representation is present but causally idle during automatic processing.
walkthrough:
The figure has three tiers. The top tier shows the same short Spanish passage inside four prompts, one per task condition of the [[language-passage-tasks]]. The middle tier gives, below each transcript, two answers: the model's answer under natural conditions, and its answer after an intervention. The bottom tier aggregates over $n=8$ passages in three panels.

The four conditions differ only in what the prompt asks. *Continuation* asks the model to write the passage's next line, a routine task that still depends on the language, since the next line of a Spanish passage must be Spanish. *Anomaly detection* splices in a sentence from another language and asks whether anything is out of place. *Explicit report* asks the model to name the language. *Flexible computation* asks for a fact about the language that the passage does not contain, such as a famous author, the word for "hello," or the pre-Euro currency; the model must identify the language first and then apply whatever function the prompt names.

In each transcript, the model's output is printed in bold, and a token is shaded wherever the token Spanish appears among the top 3 entries of the [[jacobian-lens]] readout at that position. Shading therefore marks where the language is represented in the [[j-space]], independent of whether it is used. The intervention is a [[lens-coordinate-swap]] across the question tokens, exchanging the lens coordinate for Spanish with the one for French.

Shading appears in all four transcripts; panel (b) confirms across eight passages that the language name is present in the readouts at comparable rates in every condition. Panel (a) confirms the model performs each task correctly under natural conditions. Panel (c) carries the result. Under the swap, "Spanish" becomes "French," "[Gabriel] García Márquez" becomes "[Victor] Hugo," "Hola" becomes "Bonjour," and "Peseta" becomes "Franc" — on essentially every trial. The continuation stays fluent Spanish, and the anomaly is still detected, even though the workspace now says French. This is the paper's [[flexible-vs-automatic-dissociation]] in one stimulus: presence in the workspace is uniform, causal dependence on it is not.

terms.definition: The task of writing the next line of the passage. It depends on the language but is performed routinely, and the paper classes it as automatic processing.
A sentence from a different language is spliced into the passage and the model is asked whether anything is out of place. A local coherence judgment the paper also classes as automatic.
The model is asked to name the passage's language directly. One of the two condition types the paper predicts should route through the workspace.

The model is asked for a fact about the language that the passage does not state — a famous author, the word for "hello," the pre-Euro currency — so the identified language must be handed to an arbitrary downstream function.
A token is shaded where the token Spanish appears among the top 3 entries of the J-lens readout at that position, marking where the language is represented regardless of use.
The read operation of the Jacobian lens: a score over the vocabulary computed from the residual stream at a position, whose top entries name the concepts active there.

The intervention below each transcript: at the question tokens, the activation's coordinate along the Spanish lens vector is exchanged with the coordinate along the French one, overwriting the workspace's language while leaving the passage itself untouched.
Bold text in each transcript is what the model generated; the surrounding plain text is the prompt and passage.
The unmodified forward pass, with no swap applied; the first of the two answers printed below each transcript.
The tokens of the task instruction, as opposed to the passage tokens; the swap is applied across these positions only.
Task accuracy across the eight passages: the model performs each of the four tasks correctly under natural conditions, so any difference between conditions is not a difference in competence.
The rate at which the language name appears in the J-lens readouts, per condition: comparable in all four, so workspace presence does not separate the tasks.

The rate at which the answer follows the swapped-in language: near-total for explicit report and flexible computation, near zero for continuation and anomaly detection. This panel carries the dissociation.
The region of activation space spanned by sparse nonnegative combinations of J-lens vectors — the candidate workspace whose causal role this figure tests.

numbers.meaning: Task conditions posed over the same passage: continuation, anomaly detection, explicit report, and flexible computation. Chosen so that all four depend on the language but only the last two should, on the paper's account, require the workspace.
The readout depth used for shading: a token is shaded when Spanish is among the three highest-scoring entries of the J-lens readout at that position.

The number of passages the bottom-row panels aggregate over. The single Spanish transcript at the top is one of these eight; the section states the panel-c flips occur on essentially every trial across them.

Answers printed below each transcript: one under natural conditions and one after the Spanish → French swap. The pairs "Spanish"/"French," "García Márquez"/"Hugo," "Hola"/"Bonjour," and "Peseta"/"Franc" flip; the continuation and the anomaly verdict ("Yes" in both) do not.
Bottom-row panels: (a) task accuracy, (b) presence of the language name in the readouts, (c) whether the answer follows the swapped lens value.
